name: Online Evals and Drift Alerts
question: Is quality slipping on live traffic right now?
summary: Score live traffic continuously: cheap deterministic checks on every trace, and an LLM judge on a small random sample. Track the scores and the input distribution over time windows, and alert when a score falls below a threshold or the inputs drift. Online evals catch what offline suites cannot: new user behaviour, provider changes and data drift.
useCases: Any production agent whose inputs or dependencies change over time
Quality that users notice before dashboards do
Offline eval sets that were written months ago

items.detail: schema valid, citation present, no PII leaked: run on every trace
an LLM judge on 1–5% of traces, calibrated as in Panel 1
thumbs down, escalations to a human, repeat questions
metric, window, threshold and a minimum sample size
population stability index: under 0.1 stable, 0.1–0.25 moderate, over 0.25 significant
failed live traces become new offline test cases

steps: Run cheap checks on every trace and a judge on a random sample
Aggregate scores in windows with a minimum sample size
Alert on a threshold below the baseline, tuned for few false alarms
Turn every confirmed failure into an offline test case
pitfalls: A window too small to be stable: alerts fire on noise and get ignored
A judge nobody calibrated against human labels
Alerting on averages only, so a failing segment is hidden by the rest
remember: Check everything cheaply, judge a sample, alert on windows.
caption: Illustrative: a daily judge pass rate on a 2% sample falls from about 92% to 86% after day 7.

steps.title: Choose rate, window and threshold
steps.text: Judge 2% of traffic, aggregate over 6 hours, require at least 200 judged answers, and alert on a drop of more than 4 points. These four numbers decide how noisy and how fast the alert is.

steps.title: Cheap checks on every trace
steps.text: Format and citation checks cost nothing, so they run on every answer and catch hard failures at once.

steps.title: Judge a random sample
steps.text: A calibrated LLM judge scores about 1 answer in 50. Random sampling keeps the estimate unbiased; judging everything would cost fifty times more.

steps.title: Aggregate in a window
steps.text: Over 6 hours, 2% of 12,500 answers gives 250 judgements: enough for a standard error of about 1.7 points.

steps.title: Alert with examples
steps.text: If the pass rate is more than 4 points below baseline, page someone, with links to failing traces so triage starts from evidence.

steps.title: Watch the inputs too
steps.text: Compare this window’s intent mix with the last 28 days using the population stability index. Above 0.25 the inputs have shifted, even if scores have not moved yet.

playgroundGuide.scenario: An EdTech homework-help agent answers 50,000 questions a day with a judge pass rate of about 92%. On day 8 the pass rate really drops to 86%. Tune the judge sample rate, the alert window and the threshold so the alert is quiet on normal days, quick on bad ones and affordable.
controls: Pick the judge sample rate: 0.5%, 1%, 2% or 5% of answers.
Pick the alert window: 1, 6 or 24 hours.
Pick the threshold: alert when the pass rate is more than 2, 4, 6 or 8 points below baseline.

missions.hint: Bigger windows and more judgements cut noise; the threshold must stay below the 6-point drop.

missions.text: Do the same for ₹400 a day or less.
missions.hint: 2% judging with a 6-hour window and a 4-point threshold is enough.

missions.text: Find a setting with almost no false alerts (under 0.1 a week) that takes two days or more to catch the drop.
missions.hint: Make the threshold as large as the drop, or larger, with a long window.

practice.scenario: An EdTech company’s homework-help agent answers 50,000 questions a day. Every answer gets cheap checks: valid format, a cited source, no personal data. A calibrated LLM judge scores a random 2% sample. When the 6-hour judge pass rate falls 4 points below its baseline with at least 200 judged answers, the on-call engineer is paged.

practice.analogy: A factory quality inspector. Every item gets a quick visual check; a few from each batch go to the lab.

library.name: Langfuse
library.what: Open-source LLM observability with traces, scores, datasets and LLM-as-a-judge evaluators that can run on sampled production traces.

practice.note: Scoring in your observability tool keeps scores next to the traces, so an alert links straight to failing examples.

samples.code:
import math, random
from langfuse import get_client

langfuse = get_client()
JUDGE_RATE = 0.02

def on_answer(trace_id: str, question: str, answer: str):
    langfuse.create_score(trace_id=trace_id, name="has_citation",
                          value=1.0 if "[source:" in answer else 0.0)
    if random.random() < JUDGE_RATE:                       # judge a random sample
        verdict = judge(question, answer)                  # your calibrated LLM judge
        langfuse.create_score(trace_id=trace_id, name="judge_pass",
                              value=1.0 if verdict else 0.0)

def psi(expected: dict, actual: dict, eps=1e-6) -> float:
    """Population stability index between two category distributions."""
    return sum((actual.get(k, eps) - e) * math.log(actual.get(k, eps) / e)
               for k, e in expected.items())

def should_page(pass_rate, baseline, n, min_n=200, max_drop=0.04):
    return n >= min_n and baseline - pass_rate > max_drop

numericDrill.question: Your agent answers 50,000 questions a day, evenly over 24 hours. A judge scores a random 2% sample. How many judged answers fall in one 6-hour alert window?
numericDrill.answer: 50,000 ÷ 24 × 6 = 12,500 answers per window; 2% of that is 250 judged answers. With a 92% pass rate the standard error is about √(0.92 × 0.08 ÷ 250) ≈ 1.7 points, so a 4-point threshold is about 2.3 standard errors.

interview.question: How is an online eval different from the offline suite?
interview.answer: The offline suite runs fixed test cases before a release; online evals score real traffic after it, continuously. Online evals catch new user behaviour, provider changes and drift the test set never covered, and their failures should be added back to the offline suite.

interview.question: How do you stop drift alerts from becoming noise?
interview.answer: Use windows large enough for stable estimates, a minimum sample size, thresholds set from the metric’s normal variation, and alerts per important segment rather than only a global average. Review every alert and retune rules that fire without a real problem.

mistakes.mistake: Alerting on every dip in a 15-minute window
mistakes.fix: Use a window and minimum sample large enough to be stable

mistakes.mistake: Running the judge on 100% of traffic
mistakes.fix: Check everything cheaply and judge a random sample

quiz.question: A homework-help agent answers 40,000 questions a day, evenly spread. A judge scores 1% of them. How many judged answers fall in a 12-hour window?
In that setup, each judgement costs ₹0.50. What does judging cost per day?
quiz.explanation: 1% of 40,000 is 400 judgements × ₹0.50 = ₹200 a day.

quiz.question: A window has 400 judged answers with a 90% pass rate. Roughly what is the standard error of the pass rate?
Offline evals pass, but claims staff report worse summaries. Which is the most useful next step?
options: Score a sample of live traffic and compare it with the baseline
quiz.explanation: The offline suite may not reflect today’s inputs; live scoring shows what users actually get.

quiz.question: Which checks are cheap enough to run on every production answer? Select all that apply.
options: A required citation marker is present
quiz.explanation: Deterministic checks cost almost nothing; judges and humans are for samples.

quiz.question: An alert on a 15-minute window fires several times a week with nothing wrong. What is the most likely cause?
options: The window holds too few judgements, so noise crosses the threshold
quiz.explanation: Small samples have large standard errors; widen the window or require a minimum sample.

quiz.question: The intent mix moves from {returns 60%, orders 40%} to {returns 40%, orders 60%}. Using PSI = Σ (actual − expected) × ln(actual ÷ expected), roughly what is the PSI?
quiz.explanation: Each term is 0.2 × ln(1.5) ≈ 0.081, so PSI ≈ 0.16: a moderate shift.

quiz.question: A common rule of thumb reads PSI above which value as a significant distribution shift?
quiz.explanation: Under 0.1 is usually stable, 0.1 to 0.25 moderate, above 0.25 significant.

quiz.question: A health-information agent’s judge is being set up for online scoring. What should be true before its scores drive alerts? Select all that apply.
options: It has been calibrated against human labels
Its sample is random, not hand-picked
It uses the same model as the agent
quiz.explanation: A calibrated judge on a random sample gives unbiased, trustworthy estimates.

quiz.question: Why alert on scores per important segment, such as intent or language, and not only on the global average?
options: A failing segment can hide inside a healthy average
quiz.explanation: A 20-point drop in a 10% segment moves the average only 2 points.

quiz.question: An online eval confirms that a set of claim types now fails. What should happen to those cases?
options: Add them to the offline eval suite
Ignore them once the alert clears
quiz.explanation: Failing live cases make the offline suite more representative for the next release.

quiz.question: A brokerage wants faster detection without more false alerts. Which changes help? Select all that apply.
options: Judge a larger sample, so each window is more precise
Use a window long enough for a stable estimate but short enough to react
Alert on every single failed answer
quiz.explanation: More judgements and a well-chosen window reduce noise; tiny thresholds and per-answer alerts increase it.

quiz.question: With a 24-hour window and an 8-point threshold, false alerts vanish, but a real 6-point drop takes days to catch. Why?
options: The threshold is larger than the drop, so each window rarely crosses it
quiz.explanation: A threshold above the true drop means only noisy windows cross it, so detection is slow.

quiz.question: What does an online eval add that user thumbs-down signals alone do not?
options: A consistent, unbiased quality estimate, since few users click and those who do are not typical
quiz.explanation: Feedback is sparse and self-selected; a sampled judge measures quality systematically.

quiz.question: Which belong in an alert rule for online evals? Select all that apply.
options: A threshold relative to baseline and a minimum sample size
quiz.explanation: Metric, window, threshold and minimum sample define when a page is justified.

quiz.question: A logistics agent’s judge pass rate is steady, but PSI on request types jumps to 0.31 after a new customer onboards. What is the best reading?
options: Nothing to act on because scores are fine
Inputs have shifted significantly; check quality on the new request types before it shows in the average
quiz.explanation: Drift often precedes a quality drop on the new kinds of request.

quiz.question: A support team judges 100% of traffic with an LLM judge. What is the main downside?
options: The cost scales with all traffic, when a random sample would estimate quality almost as well
It removes the need for a baseline
quiz.explanation: Sampling gives nearly the same estimate at a small fraction of the cost.

quiz.question: Which could explain a drop in live quality while offline evals still pass? Select all that apply.
options: Users started asking kinds of questions missing from the test set
The provider changed the snapshot behind an alias
The offline suite ran after the change and caught it
quiz.explanation: New inputs and silent model changes both escape a fixed, earlier offline run.

quiz.question: Where should an online-eval page link to, so triage starts fast?
options: The failing traces behind the drop
quiz.explanation: Linking to failing examples lets the engineer see what broke immediately.

quiz.question: Which settings reduce judge cost without making the alert blind? Select all that apply.
options: Sample a fixed percentage chosen for enough judgements per window
Run cheap deterministic checks on everything and the judge only on a sample
Judge only answers that users already liked
quiz.explanation: A sized sample plus cheap checks keeps cost low and coverage honest; biased or gapped sampling does not.
